passages.title: The cross challenges ownership of another believer
passages.summary: Paul and Sosthenes write to the assembly of God at Corinth. Paul thanks God for their gifts of speech and knowledge. Then he begs them to agree, for Chloe’s people report quarrels. Some say they follow Paul, and others Apollos, Cephas, or Christ. Paul is glad he baptized only a few of them. He says the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing. Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but he announces Christ crucified. God chose the weak and lowly, so no one may boast.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers show the receiving church, recalled settings, and intended destinations. No exact household or journey is assigned.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches unity in Christ’s Church. Why does Paul answer competing party names with questions about baptism and crucifixion?

contextNote.title: The cross challenges ownership of another believer
contextNote.text: Verse 12 quotes four slogans: of Paul, of Apollos, of Cephas, of Christ. Verse 13 answers with three questions, and each expects “no.” Christ is not divided. Paul was not crucified for them. They were not baptized into Paul’s name. No party leader died for them or gave them a name. Verses 14–15 add that Paul baptized few, so no one can claim his name.

passages.title: Paul's remembered weakness refuses to make eloquence the source of faith
passages.summary: Paul recalls his first visit to Corinth. He did not come with fine speech or wisdom. He decided to know nothing among them but Jesus Christ crucified. He was weak, afraid, and trembling. Yet he says there is a wisdom for the mature, hidden and now revealed. The rulers of this age did not know it and crucified the Lord. God’s Spirit reveals what God has given. The natural person does not receive these things, but “we have Christ’s mind.”

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches reliance on God’s wisdom. Why does Paul recall his fear rather than present an impressive speaking record?

contextNote.title: Paul's remembered weakness refuses to make eloquence the source of faith
contextNote.text: Chapter 1 said the Corinthians were dividing over teachers. Paul answers with how he first spoke to them (verses 1–4). He had no fine speech, and he came in weakness and fear. Verse 5 gives the purpose behind that. Faith that rests on a speaker’s skill rests on human wisdom. He wanted theirs to rest on God’s power. Verse 4 names where that power showed: in the Spirit, not in persuasive words.

passages.title: Different workers serve growth they cannot produce themselves
passages.summary: Paul says he fed the Corinthians milk, because they were not ready for solid food. Their jealousy and quarrels show they are still fleshly. Paul and Apollos are only servants. One planted and one watered, but God gave the growth. Paul laid a foundation, which is Jesus Christ, and others build on it. Fire will test each builder’s work. The believers are God’s temple, and God’s Spirit lives in them. So no one should boast in men, for all things are theirs.

lds.text: The selected lesson uses God’s building to teach shared work and unity. How do planting and watering differ from giving growth?

contextNote.title: Different workers serve growth they cannot produce themselves
contextNote.text: Verse 4 repeats the slogans: “I follow Paul” and “I follow Apollos.” Verse 5 asks what these men are, and answers “servants.” Verse 6 gives each his task in three short sentences. Paul planted, Apollos watered, and God gave the increase. Only the third makes anything grow. Verse 7 draws the result: planter and waterer are nothing beside God. Verse 8 adds that the planter and the waterer are one.

passages.title: Received gifts cannot support boasting as though nothing was given
passages.summary: Paul calls himself a servant of Christ and a steward of God’s mysteries. A steward must be faithful, and the Lord is the judge. He tells them not to be puffed up for one teacher against another. He says they act as if they already reign as kings. The apostles, he says, are like men sentenced to death. They are hungry, beaten, homeless, and treated as the world’s filth. Paul writes as a father to warn his children. He is sending Timothy and plans to come himself.

lds.text: What does the question about received gifts expose in the hearers’ boasting?

contextNote.title: Received gifts cannot support boasting as though nothing was given
contextNote.text: Verse 6 names the problem: being puffed up for one against another. Verse 7 answers with three questions. Who makes you different? What do you have that you did not receive? If you received it, why boast as if you had not? Each question removes a ground for pride. Verses 8–13 then set their boast beside the apostles’ hunger and insults.

passages.title: The boundary concerns claimed membership rather than leaving the whole world
passages.summary: Paul has heard that a man in the assembly lives with his father’s wife. He says even the Gentiles do not accept this. The assembly is proud when it should mourn. Paul tells them to gather and remove the man. A little yeast leavens the whole lump, and Christ is their Passover. He explains an earlier letter. He did not mean to avoid immoral people of the world. He meant one called a brother who lives that way.

lds.text: Why does Paul distinguish the group’s own boundary from judgment outside?

contextNote.title: The boundary concerns claimed membership rather than leaving the whole world
contextNote.text: An earlier letter said not to keep company with the sexually immoral (verse 9). It could be read as meaning everyone. Verse 10 says that would require leaving the world. Verse 11 limits it to one “who is called a brother.” Verse 12 gives the reason in two questions. Paul has no task of judging outsiders; the assembly judges those within. Verse 13 leaves outsiders to God and tells them to remove the man.

passages.title: Claimed freedom fails when it becomes another form of control
passages.summary: Paul rebukes believers who take one another to court before unbelievers. He asks if no one among them is wise enough to decide. It would be better to be wronged. He lists those who will not inherit God’s kingdom. He says some of them were such, but they were washed and made holy. Then he answers the saying that all things are lawful. The body is for the Lord and will be raised. It is a temple of the Holy Spirit, bought with a price.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches that physical bodies are sacred. How can an action claimed as freedom become a source of control?

contextNote.title: Claimed freedom fails when it becomes another form of control
contextNote.text: The saying “All things are lawful for me” stands twice in verse 12. Paul does not deny it; he adds two limits. Not all things are helpful. He also will not be brought under the power of anything. The second limit turns the saying around. A freedom that masters its user is no longer freedom. Verses 19–20 give the ground: the body is not one’s own.

passages.title: Paul distinguishes commands from advice shaped by present distress
passages.summary: Paul answers questions the Corinthians wrote to him about marriage. Husband and wife owe each other their bodies. The married should not separate, and he says this command is the Lord’s. A believer should stay with an unbelieving spouse who is willing. Each should remain in the state in which he was called. About the unmarried, Paul gives his own judgment. Because of the present distress it is good to remain as they are. Yet one who marries does not sin.

lds.text: Why does Paul distinguish commands from his own judgment about unmarried life?

contextNote.title: Paul distinguishes commands from advice shaped by present distress
contextNote.text: Paul marks his sources through the chapter. Verse 10 is the Lord’s command. Verse 12 is Paul’s own word, “not the Lord.” Verse 25 says he has no command about virgins and gives a judgment. Verse 35 says how to take that judgment. It is for their benefit, and it is not a snare to hold them. Its aim is attention to the Lord without distraction, as verses 32–34 explain.

passages.title: Knowledge must consider the person whom freedom can wound
passages.summary: Paul turns to food sacrificed to idols. He says knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. An idol is nothing, and there is one God and one Lord. Not everyone has that knowledge. Some still think of the idol when they eat, and their conscience suffers. Food does not bring anyone nearer to God. A weak believer may see another eat in an idol’s temple and follow. Paul says he would never eat meat if it made a brother stumble.

lds.text: How does the observer’s conscience change the confident believer’s food choice?

contextNote.title: Knowledge must consider the person whom freedom can wound
contextNote.text: Verses 4–6 grant the point of those with knowledge: an idol is nothing. Verse 8 grants that food changes nothing before God. Verse 9 then begins with “but.” The right is real, yet it can trip the weak. Verse 10 gives the case: a weak person sees and copies against conscience. Verse 11 counts the cost: a brother for whom Christ died is destroyed. Verse 12 calls this a sin against Christ.

passages.title: A right can remain valid even when its holder refuses to use it
passages.summary: Paul asks if he is not free and an apostle. He says he has the right to food, drink, and support. A soldier, a vinedresser, and a shepherd all live from their work. The law says not to muzzle an ox that treads grain. Yet Paul has not used this right. He offers the good news free of charge. He becomes as a Jew to Jews and weak to the weak. He trains like a runner so that he is not disqualified.

lds.text: The selected lesson cites Paul’s instruction about support for gospel teachers. Why does Paul defend a right that he chooses not to use?

contextNote.title: A right can remain valid even when its holder refuses to use it
contextNote.text: Chapter 8 asked the knowing to give up a right for the weak. Chapter 9 shows Paul doing the same with his own right. Verses 4–11 prove that he may be supported. Verse 12 says others use this right over the Corinthians. Then it says he did not use it. His reason is in the same verse: no hindrance to the good news. Verse 14 keeps the right in force, as something the Lord ordained.

passages.title: Food choices depend on setting and another person's good
passages.summary: Paul recalls Israel in the wilderness. All passed through the sea and ate the same spiritual food, yet most fell. These things are examples and warnings. God will not let them be tempted beyond their strength. Paul tells them to flee idolatry. They cannot share the Lord’s table and the table of demons. Meat from the market may be eaten without questions. If someone says it was offered to idols, they should not eat.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches escape from temptation and unity through the sacrament. Why does an explicit notice about food change the invited meal?

contextNote.title: Food choices depend on setting and another person's good
contextNote.text: Verse 23 repeats “All things are lawful” and adds that not all build up. Verse 24 gives the rule for the cases that follow. Seek the neighbor’s good, not your own. Verses 25–27 apply it one way: eat market meat and a host’s food freely. Verses 28–29 apply it the other way. If someone points out idol food, refrain for that person’s conscience. The food is the same; the neighbor’s good decides.

passages.title: Remembering the shared meal exposes the shame caused by private advantage
passages.summary: Paul gives instructions about head coverings when men and women pray or prophesy. He then turns to their shared meal and does not praise them. There are divisions when they meet. Each eats his own supper first, so one is hungry and another is drunk. Paul repeats what he received about the Lord’s bread and cup. Whoever eats in an unworthy way is guilty concerning the Lord’s body and blood. Each should examine himself. When they come together to eat, they should wait for one another.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects self examination and the sacrament with unity. How does waiting for others answer the shame caused by unequal eating?

contextNote.title: Remembering the shared meal exposes the shame caused by private advantage
contextNote.text: Verse 21 describes the fault: each takes his own supper before others. One goes hungry, and another is drunk. Verse 22 says this shames those who have nothing. Paul then recalls the Lord’s words over bread and cup (verses 23–25). Verse 33 gives the practical order that follows from them. They are to wait for one another. ancientRoads.title: Appian Way
ancientRoads.summary: The Appian Way joined Rome with Capua and the port of Brundisium. Rome began it in 312 BCE.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 28:15 says believers met Paul at the Market of Appius and Three Taverns. Both were stops on this road south of Rome.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The road’s course is well known. The line joins its main towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Egnatia
ancientRoads.summary: Rome built this road across Macedonia in the second century BCE. It ran from the Adriatic coast to Thessalonica and on to Byzantium.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 16:11–17:1 takes Paul through Neapolis, Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica. The encyclopedia article places that trip on this road.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones mark the road as far as the edge of Thrace. The line joins known towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Sebaste
ancientRoads.summary: Rome finished this army road in 6 BCE. It climbed from Perga on the coast to Antioch of Pisidia. A branch reached Iconium and Lystra.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 13:14 takes Paul from Perga to Antioch of Pisidia. He may have used this road, but Acts does not say.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones fix parts of the road. The line between the towns is simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Cilician Gates pass
ancientRoads.summary: This pass crosses the Taurus Mountains north of Tarsus. It joins the plain of Cilicia with the high plateau.
ancientRoads.detail: Armies and traders used the pass for a very long time. Acts 15:41 sends Paul through Cilicia but does not name the pass.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass is certain. The line beyond it is a broad guide.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.

regions.name: Judea · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome removed Herod’s son Archelaus in 6 CE and made Judea a province. Its governor lived at Caesarea on the coast.
regions.detail: Governors Felix and Festus hold Paul at Caesarea (Acts 23–26). Acts 12 names an earlier ruler King Herod; historians call him Agrippa I.

regions.name: Syria · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
regions.detail: Believers are first called Christians at Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26). Antioch sends out Barnabas and Saul in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Cilicia · approximate
regions.summary: Cilicia lay on the south coast of Asia Minor. Rome took it in 64 BCE.
regions.detail: Paul comes from Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21:39). He passes through Syria and Cilicia in Acts 15:41.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows the eastern plain around Tarsus only.

regions.name: Cyprus · Roman province
regions.summary: Cyprus was a Roman province under a proconsul. Paphos was its capital.
regions.detail: Barnabas comes from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). He and Saul cross the island from Salamis to Paphos in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape follows the modern coast of the island.

regions.name: Galatia · Roman province
regions.summary: Augustus made Galatia a province in 25 BCE. Ancyra was its capital.
regions.detail: Paul writes to the assemblies of Galatia. Acts 13–14 places him at Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Pamphylia on the south coast belonged to Galatia for a time.

regions.name: Asia · Roman province
regions.summary: Asia was a rich Roman province in western Asia Minor. A proconsul governed it.
regions.detail: Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years (Acts 19:10). Revelation 1–3 writes to seven assemblies in Asia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Bithynia and Pontus · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome joined Bithynia and Pontus into one province on the Black Sea coast.
regions.detail: The Spirit keeps Paul from entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7). First Peter greets believers in Pontus and Bithynia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the coast lands.

regions.name: Cappadocia · Roman province
regions.summary: Cappadocia became a Roman province in 17 CE. Its capital was a city named Caesarea.
regions.detail: People from Cappadocia hear Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). First Peter 1:1 greets believers there.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. This Caesarea is not the port in Judea.

regions.name: Macedonia · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Macedonia a province in 146 BCE. The Via Egnatia crossed it from west to east.
regions.detail: A vision calls Paul to Macedonia (Acts 16:9). He teaches in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Beroea.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It includes Thessaly and Epirus, which the province held.

regions.name: Achaia · Roman province
regions.summary: Achaia covered southern Greece. Augustus made it a province apart from Macedonia.
regions.detail: Paul speaks in Athens and stays in Corinth (Acts 17–18). Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, hears a charge against him.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The province’s islands are not marked.

regions.name: Crete · part of a Roman province
regions.summary: Rome governed Crete together with Cyrenaica in North Africa.
regions.detail: Paul’s ship shelters along Crete in Acts 27. Paul leaves Titus in Crete to appoint elders (Titus 1:5).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the island. Cyrenaica is not marked.

regions.name: Italy
regions.summary: Italy was the home region of Rome. It had a special status among Roman lands.
regions.detail: Paul lands at Puteoli and goes on to Rome (Acts 28). Hebrews 13:24 sends greetings from the Italians.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the peninsula.

guides.title: 1 Corinthians: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Different workers serve growth they cannot produce themselves
steps.text: Verse 4 repeats the slogans: “I follow Paul” and “I follow Apollos.” Verse 5 asks what these men are, and answers “servants.” Verse 6 gives each his task in three short sentences. Paul planted, Apollos watered, and God gave the increase. Only the third makes anything grow. Verse 7 draws the result: planter and waterer are nothing beside God. Verse 8 adds that the planter and the waterer are one.

steps.title: Knowledge must consider the person whom freedom can wound
steps.text: Verses 4–6 grant the point of those with knowledge: an idol is nothing. Verse 8 grants that food changes nothing before God. Verse 9 then begins with “but.” The right is real, yet it can trip the weak. Verse 10 gives the case: a weak person sees and copies against conscience. Verse 11 counts the cost: a brother for whom Christ died is destroyed. Verse 12 calls this a sin against Christ.

steps.title: Remembering the shared meal exposes the shame caused by private advantage
steps.text: Verse 21 describes the fault: each takes his own supper before others. One goes hungry, and another is drunk. Verse 22 says this shames those who have nothing. Paul then recalls the Lord’s words over bread and cup (verses 23–25). Verse 33 gives the practical order that follows from them. They are to wait for one another. Verse 34 adds that anyone hungry should eat at home first.

steps.title: Resurrection gives present labor a future beyond death
steps.text: Verses 12–19 follow one claim to its end. If the dead are not raised, Christ is not raised. Then faith is useless, and the dead in Christ have perished (verses 17–18). Verse 20 breaks in with “But now.” Christ has been raised, and he is called the first fruit. A first fruit is the first part of a harvest, with more to come. Verse 23 gives the order: Christ first, then those who are his.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul and Sosthenes write to the assembly of God at Corinth. Paul thanks God for their gifts of speech and knowledge. Then he begs them to agree, for Chloe’s people report quarrels. Some say they follow Paul, and others Apollos, Cephas, or Christ. Paul is glad he baptized only a few of them. He says the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing. Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but he announces Christ crucified. God chose the weak and lowly, so no one may boast.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul recalls his first visit to Corinth. He did not come with fine speech or wisdom. He decided to know nothing among them but Jesus Christ crucified. He was weak, afraid, and trembling. Yet he says there is a wisdom for the mature, hidden and now revealed. The rulers of this age did not know it and crucified the Lord. God’s Spirit reveals what God has given. The natural person does not receive these things, but “we have Christ’s mind.”

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says he fed the Corinthians milk, because they were not ready for solid food. Their jealousy and quarrels show they are still fleshly. Paul and Apollos are only servants. One planted and one watered, but God gave the growth. Paul laid a foundation, which is Jesus Christ, and others build on it. Fire will test each builder’s work. The believers are God’s temple, and God’s Spirit lives in them. So no one should boast in men, for all things are theirs.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul calls himself a servant of Christ and a steward of God’s mysteries. A steward must be faithful, and the Lord is the judge. He tells them not to be puffed up for one teacher against another. He says they act as if they already reign as kings. The apostles, he says, are like men sentenced to death. They are hungry, beaten, homeless, and treated as the world’s filth. Paul writes as a father to warn his children. He is sending Timothy and plans to come himself.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul has heard that a man in the assembly lives with his father’s wife. He says even the Gentiles do not accept this. The assembly is proud when it should mourn. Paul tells them to gather and remove the man. A little yeast leavens the whole lump, and Christ is their Passover. He explains an earlier letter. He did not mean to avoid immoral people of the world. He meant one called a brother who lives that way.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul rebukes believers who take one another to court before unbelievers. He asks if no one among them is wise enough to decide. It would be better to be wronged. He lists those who will not inherit God’s kingdom. He says some of them were such, but they were washed and made holy. Then he answers the saying that all things are lawful. The body is for the Lord and will be raised. It is a temple of the Holy Spirit, bought with a price.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul answers questions the Corinthians wrote to him about marriage. Husband and wife owe each other their bodies. The married should not separate, and he says this command is the Lord’s. A believer should stay with an unbelieving spouse who is willing. Each should remain in the state in which he was called. About the unmarried, Paul gives his own judgment. Because of the present distress it is good to remain as they are. Yet one who marries does not sin.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul turns to food sacrificed to idols. He says knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. An idol is nothing, and there is one God and one Lord. Not everyone has that knowledge. Some still think of the idol when they eat, and their conscience suffers. Food does not bring anyone nearer to God. A weak believer may see another eat in an idol’s temple and follow. Paul says he would never eat meat if it made a brother stumble.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul asks if he is not free and an apostle. He says he has the right to food, drink, and support. A soldier, a vinedresser, and a shepherd all live from their work. The law says not to muzzle an ox that treads grain. Yet Paul has not used this right. He offers the good news free of charge. He becomes as a Jew to Jews and weak to the weak. He trains like a runner so that he is not disqualified.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul recalls Israel in the wilderness. All passed through the sea and ate the same spiritual food, yet most fell. These things are examples and warnings. God will not let them be tempted beyond their strength. Paul tells them to flee idolatry. They cannot share the Lord’s table and the table of demons. Meat from the market may be eaten without questions. If someone says it was offered to idols, they should not eat.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul gives instructions about head coverings when men and women pray or prophesy. He then turns to their shared meal and does not praise them. There are divisions when they meet. Each eats his own supper first, so one is hungry and another is drunk. Paul repeats what he received about the Lord’s bread and cup. Whoever eats in an unworthy way is guilty concerning the Lord’s body and blood. Each should examine himself. When they come together to eat, they should wait for one another.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul writes about spiritual gifts. There are different gifts, services, and workings, but the same Spirit, Lord, and God. Each receives a gift for the good of all. Paul lists wisdom, knowledge, faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, languages, and more. He compares the assembly to one body with many members. A foot cannot say it does not belong, and an eye cannot dismiss a hand. If one member suffers, all suffer. God has set apostles, prophets, teachers, and others in the assembly.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says languages of men and angels are noise without love. Prophecy, knowledge, and faith that moves mountains are nothing without it. Giving away everything gains nothing without it. He then says what love does. It is patient and kind, and it does not envy, brag, or seek its own. It bears, believes, hopes, and endures all things. Prophecy, languages, and knowledge will end, but love never fails. Faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest is love.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul tells them to follow love and to desire prophecy most. One who speaks in another language speaks to God, and no one understands. One who prophesies builds up the assembly. A trumpet with an unclear sound calls no one to battle. Paul would rather speak five words with understanding than ten thousand in another language. At most two or three should speak in another language, with an interpreter. Prophets should speak in turn while others weigh it. God is a God of peace, and all should be done in order.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul repeats the good news he delivered. Christ died for sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day. He appeared to Cephas, the twelve, five hundred others, James, and Paul. Some in Corinth say there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul says that if so, Christ was not raised and faith is empty. But Christ has been raised, the first fruit of those who sleep. The body is sown perishable and raised imperishable, like a seed. Death is swallowed up, so their labor is not in vain.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul gives directions for the collection for the saints. Each should set money aside on the first day of the week. Approved people will carry the gift to Jerusalem. Paul plans to come through Macedonia and stay in Ephesus until Pentecost. He asks them to receive Timothy without fear and says Apollos will come later. He tells them to watch, stand firm, and do everything in love. He commends the household of Stephanas. He signs the greeting with his own hand.
